title: Upbeat Nystagmus (UBN): A Clinical Masterclass
summary: Upbeat nystagmus is a vertical jerk nystagmus characterized by a fast upward phase in primary position, typically localizing to the brainstem or cerebellar vermis. This infographic provides a comprehensive guide to its neuro-anatomical localization, etiology, and evidence-based management.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Upbeat nystagmus (UBN) is a primary position vertical jerk nystagmus with the fast phase directed superiorly. It is an acquired ocular motor disorder that often violates Alexander's Law, typically increasing in intensity on upgaze. It results from an imbalance in the vertical vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) or a defect in the vertical neural integrator.

rows: Wallenberg Syndrome (Lateral Medullary Infarction), PICA or AICA stroke, Thalamic hemorrhage.
Medulloblastoma, Astrocytoma, Paraneoplastic syndromes (Anti-Yo, Anti-Hu antibodies).
Lithium toxicity, Phenytoin, Carbamazepine, Alcohol intoxication, Tobacco-alcohol amblyopia.

sections.title: Pathophysiology: Why does it happen?
content: Imbalance in Vertical VOR: Selective damage to the posterior semicircular canal pathways (which mediate downward slow phases).
Neural Integrator Failure: Damage to the Interstitial Nucleus of Cajal (INC) or the Nucleus Prepositus Hypoglossi (NPH) leads to a 'leaky' integrator.
Primary Position Instability: The slow phase drifts downward due to gravity or tonic imbalance, triggering a corrective upward fast phase.
Cerebellar Disinhibition: Loss of Purkinje cell inhibition from the flocculus/paraflocculus on the vestibular nuclei.

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Fast phase directed UPWARD in primary position.
Amplitude increases in UPGaze (usually).
May decrease or convert to DBN in downgaze (occasionally).
Associated with Oscillopsia (visual blurring/shaking).
Often associated with other brainstem signs (ataxia, dysarthria, Horner's syndrome).

sections.title: Critical Red Flags
content: Acute onset UBN with Ataxia & Confusion (Suspect Wernicke’s!)
Associated Papilledema (Suspect Midbrain tumor/Hydrocephalus)
Sudden 'Thunderclap' headache (Brainstem hemorrhage)
Progressive swallowing or breathing difficulties (Lower medullary compression)

content.explanation: U: Upper Medulla, P: Pons (paramedian), B: Brainstem (diffuse), E: Eye-movement Integrator (INC), A: Anterior Vermis (Cerebellum), T: Thiamine deficiency (Wernicke's).

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Protocol
content: Step 1: Neuro-ophthalmologic Exam - Confirm UBN, check for internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO) or skew deviation.
Step 2: Urgent Neuroimaging - MRI Brain with GAD + MRI Posterior Fossa (Focus on Craniocervical junction and Brainstem).
Step 3: Laboratory Testing - Serum Thiamine (B1) levels, CBC, BMP, Magnesium, Lithium levels.
Step 4: Paraneoplastic Panel - If imaging is negative and age/risk factors suggest occult malignancy.
Step 5: Lumbar Puncture - If MS or inflammatory/infectious etiology is suspected (check O-bands, cytology).

rows: NMDA receptor antagonist; helps suppress oscillation.
GABA-B agonist; particularly effective for periodic alternating or vertical nystagmus.
Calcium channel subunit ligand; reduces oscillopsia.
Potassium channel blocker; more commonly used for DBN but trial in UBN.
MANDATORY if Wernicke's suspected; give BEFORE glucose.

sections.title: Surgical & Optical Strategies
content: Base-down Prisms: Shift the image into a gaze position where the nystagmus is minimized (null zone).
Large-recess Kestenbaum: Surgical transposition of extraocular muscles to move the eyes toward the null zone (rarely used for acquired UBN).
Botulinum Toxin Injections: Retrobulbar injection can temporarily paretize muscles to reduce amplitude (last resort due to side effects).

content.explanation: If UBN is present in primary position and increases in upgaze, think Medulla. If UBN is present in primary position but increases in downgaze (or is associated with See-saw), think Midbrain.

sections.title: Prognosis & Complications
sections.content: Prognosis is entirely dependent on the underlying cause. Wernicke-related UBN can resolve rapidly with thiamine. MS-related UBN may fluctuate with relapses. Chronic UBN leads to severe reading difficulty and gait instability, significantly impacting quality of life and increasing fall risk.

sections.title: Pediatric Considerations
content: Congenital UBN: Rare; often associated with ocular albinism or Leber Congenital Amaurosis.
Neuroblastoma: Always screen for opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia syndrome.
Leigh Syndrome: Mitochondrial disorder causing brainstem lesions and vertical nystagmus.
